analysis.one_liner: Exempts stormwater runoff from logging operations from Clean Water Act permits.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the bill by voice vote and reported it in November 2014, but the full House never voted on it before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes a permanent exemption into the Clean Water Act barring the EPA from requiring a water-pollution discharge permit for stormwater runoff from logging activities — nursery operations, site preparation, reforestation, thinning, prescribed burning, pest and fire control, harvesting, surface drainage, and forest road construction and maintenance. State permitting programs could not be required either, since the bill bars the EPA from directly or indirectly requiring states to permit those discharges. Discharges of dredged or fill material remain covered under a separate Clean Water Act section. The bill cleared committee but never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Timber companies, forest landowners, and logging contractors, who would avoid federal permitting costs and the litigation exposure that comes with permit requirements for logging runoff.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA from requiring, or from directing states to require, a discharge permit for stormwater runoff from nine listed logging activities, including harvesting, surface drainage, and forest road construction and maintenance [S2][S4].
Locks the exemption into the Clean Water Act itself, so a future EPA could not restore permit requirements by regulation for those activities [S4].
Preserves permitting for dredged or fill material discharges under section 404, narrowing the exemption's reach [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: People who live downstream of logging operations, whose streams, drinking-water sources, and fisheries would get less federal oversight of sediment and pollutant runoff from logging sites and forest roads.

drawbacks.text: Logging road construction, maintenance, surface drainage, and harvesting — activities the bill exempts — are among the sources of sediment-laden runoff that degrades streams used for drinking water and fish habitat; exempting them from permits shifts all oversight to state forestry programs, whose rigor varies widely from state to state [S2][S4].
Because the exemption is written into the Clean Water Act, it is permanent and could not be undone by a future EPA without new legislation, even where state programs fail to control runoff [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: logging operators avoid federal permit paperwork, fees, and the risk of citizen lawsuits over unpermitted runoff. The cost is weaker federal oversight of a known pollution pathway into streams, with no federal backstop if a state's forestry program is weak. On balance, this is a targeted regulatory carve-out for one industry rather than a measure that helps ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee — it was reported in November 2014 and placed on the House calendar — but House leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Introduced May 16, 2013 and referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, then to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee [S1][S6].
The subcommittee was discharged on October 29, 2013, and the full committee marked up the bill and ordered it reported by voice vote the same day [S6].

The committee formally reported the bill on November 12, 2014 (H. Rept. 113-607) without amendment, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 452 — the list of bills awaiting House floor action [S3][S6].
The House never voted on the bill; the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still on the calendar [S6].
The bill carried 69 cosponsors — 54 Republicans and 15 Democrats — and had cleared committee with a voice vote, but still never reached the floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Downstream communities and anyone who relies on the existing Clean Water Act permitting framework are better off, because the statutory exemption for logging runoff was never enacted; timber operators gained nothing but lost nothing either, since current rules stayed in place.

for.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill and ordered it reported by voice vote on October 29, 2013; reported it to the House on November 12, 2014 (H. Rept. 113-607)

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was reported and placed on the Union Calendar; the Congress ended without action

against.name: Environmental and clean-water advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed a statutory exemption of logging runoff from Clean Water Act discharge permits

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan in form — 15 of the 69 cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee reported the bill by voice vote — but cosponsorship leaned heavily Republican (54 R to 15 D), and there was no recorded floor vote to break down by party.

industries.note: The bill would permanently exempt logging operations, including forest road construction and harvesting, from Clean Water Act discharge permits for stormwater runoff, saving timber operators permitting costs and shielding them from citizen enforcement suits. The savings come at the expense of reduced federal oversight of sediment runoff into streams used by the public [S2][S4].

Road construction, maintenance, and surface drainage work — core contractor activities — would be exempt from discharge permitting, reducing compliance burdens on the crews that do the cutting and roadwork [S2][S4].

industries.industry: Commercial and recreational fisheries dependent on forested streams
industries.note: Runoff from the exempted activities — harvesting, surface drainage, and road building — carries sediment into streams, so weaker permitting oversight puts fish habitat that fisheries depend on at greater risk [S2][S4].
